subject: ss-pulmonology
title: Nicotine replacement therapy in tobacco cessation

steps.tx: **Nicotine replacement therapy** (NRT) delivers nicotine without the smoke, so it eases **withdrawal** while the patient stops smoking. It raises the chance of quitting when paired with behavioural support. Available forms include patches, gum, lozenges, inhalers and nasal sprays. Patches release a steady background dose across the day, whereas gum and lozenges tackle sudden cravings quickly. Many clinicians combine a patch with a short-acting product for better results.

steps.tx: The strength of **nicotine replacement therapy** is matched to how heavily someone smokes. A **transdermal patch** is commonly started at 21 mg daily for those using more than 10 cigarettes a day, and 14 mg for lighter smokers. For **gum** or **lozenges**, the **time to first cigarette** guides the choice: 2 mg if it is over 30 minutes after waking, and 4 mg if it is within 30 minutes. Doses are then reduced gradually over several weeks.

A transdermal patch is commonly started at twenty one milligrams daily for those using more than ten cigarettes a day, and fourteen milligrams for lighter smokers. For gum or lozenges, the time to first cigarette guides the choice: two milligrams if it is over thirty minutes after waking, and four milligrams if it is within thirty minutes. Doses are then reduced gradually over several weeks.

steps.tx: Gum and lozenges must be used correctly to work. The gum is chewed slowly until a tingling taste appears, then parked between cheek and gum, repeated over about 30 minutes. A lozenge should dissolve slowly over 20 to 30 minutes rather than being chewed. Acidic drinks such as coffee, juice or cola reduce **nicotine absorption** from the mouth, so the patient should avoid them for about 15 minutes before and during use.

steps.tx: Some groups need extra caution. Severe **renal impairment** and moderate hepatic impairment slow nicotine clearance, so doses may need reducing. Older patients are usually started at the lower end of the range. Pregnant patients are first offered behavioural support, with NRT used only if that fails. NRT safety and efficacy are not established in those aged 18 or younger, so adolescents need behavioural counselling first.
